summary: Johannes Haeberlin was an Indologist. He studied at the Basel Mission Seminary in 1827 and at the Church Missionary Society College, Islington, in 1830.

Johannes Hertel was an Indologist who studied at the University of Leipzig under Ernst Windisch, earning his doctorate. He taught at Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (~1898–1919; Professor from ~1908) and held the chair of Indian philology at Leipzig (1919–1937).

Johannes Klatt was an Indologist who studied under Albrecht Weber in Berlin and completed his PhD at Halle-Wittenberg under August Friedrich Pott. From 1872, he worked at the Royal Library of Berlin, becoming custodian in 1880 and librarian in 1889.

Johannes Lohmann worked in linguistics and philosophy. After earning his doctorate and completing his habilitation under Wilhelm Schulze in Berlin, he taught in Berlin, Rostock, Basel, and Freiburg, serving as ordinary professor of comparative linguistics at Freiburg (1949–1963).
Johannes Mehlig was an Indologist who studied under Paul Thieme (~1948–1953) and Friedrich Weller (~1950–1956).

Johannes Nobel worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology. He completed his PhD under Heinrich Lüders in Berlin, where he later taught. From 1928 to 1955, he held the chair of Indology at the University of Marburg.

Johannes Rahder worked in Indology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies. He earned his PhD at Utrecht under Willem Caland and held professorships at Utrecht (1929–1931), Leiden (1931–1946), the University of Hawaiʻi (1946–1947), and Yale University (1947–1965).
Johannes Reinoud Abraham Loman was an Indologist. He completed his PhD at the University of Amsterdam (~1950–1956) under Adriaan Scharpé and held a post at Leiden University from 1958 to 1973.

Johannes Schmidt worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned his PhD at Jena under August Schleicher. He taught at Bonn and held the chair of comparative linguistics and Sanskrit at Graz (1873–1876) before becoming professor in Berlin in 1876.

Johannes Schneider is a scholar of Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies. He earned his Magister at Marburg and has held positions at Freie Universität Berlin, the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and the University of Munich, becoming apl. Professor in 2014.

Johannes Schubert specialized in Tibetology and Sinology, completing his PhD at Berlin in 1928. He served as a librarian at Leipzig University Library (1928–1954) and taught at the University of Leipzig from 1934, later serving as professor and director.

Johannes Toepffer was a scholar in history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Tartu under Leo Meyer and under Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, later holding a post at the University of Basel (~1894–1895).

John A. Ardussi works in Tibetology and history and archaeology. He studied under Turrell V. Wylie and earned a PhD from the Australian National University. His posts include Senior Research Fellow at the University of Virginia and researcher at CNRS.

John Alexander Corrie Boswell was active in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as a colonial civil servant in the Madras Civil Service (1855–1871) and was in the Indian Civil Service (~1856–1872).

John Alexander Jorgensen works in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology. He earned an MA under Kenneth H. J. Gardiner at the Australian National University, where he later became adjunct associate professor, and taught as senior lecturer at Griffith University.

John Alexander Stewart, who studied at the University of Aberdeen, worked in linguistics. After serving in the Indian Civil Service (~1905–1933), he was Reader in Burmese at the University of London (~1933–1944) and held a post at SOAS (~1933–1948).

John Allan was a scholar of Indology, history, and archaeology who studied at Edinburgh and Leipzig. He served at the British Museum (1907–1949; Deputy Keeper 1924–1949) and lectured in Sanskrit at UCL, SOAS, and the University of Edinburgh.

John Anderson was an MD graduate of Edinburgh working in history, archaeology, and Indology. He was professor of natural history at Free Church College (~1862–1864), curator/supervisor at the Indian Museum, Kolkata (1865–1886), and professor at Calcutta Medical College (1877).
John Archibald Boyle was an Indologist who was educated at Radley College until 1858. In 1865, he was appointed as a civil servant in the Madras Civil Service.

John Avery was an Indologist and linguist who studied under William Dwight Whitney at Yale and attended Amherst, Berlin, and Tübingen. He served as Professor of Greek at Grinnell College (1870–1877) and Bowdoin College (1877–1887).
